subtopics.title: Temperature, Pressure and Wind — the Chain

questions.question: Warm air at the surface produces:
options: LOW pressure — the air expands, becomes less dense and rises, so fewer molecules press on the surface
HIGH pressure, because warm air is heavier
No pressure change at all
High pressure aloft and high pressure at the surface

questions.question: Tightly packed isobars on a synoptic chart indicate:
options: Calm conditions
A steep pressure gradient and therefore strong wind
Rain but no wind
An error in plotting

questions.question: Why does a high-pressure cell bring clear, dry, settled weather?
options: The air rises and cools
Highs contain no water vapour
Air SUBSIDES, is compressed and warms adiabatically, so relative humidity falls and cloud evaporates
Highs occur only over deserts

questions.question: The 16 cardinal points are spaced how far apart, and what is the bearing of a south-easter?
options: 45 degrees apart; 090 degrees
30 degrees apart; 120 degrees
10 degrees apart; 150 degrees
22,5 degrees apart, since 360 ÷ 16 = 22,5; a south-easter blows from 135 degrees

questions.question: The subtropical high-pressure belts at about 30 degrees north and south are formed by:
options: Air that rose at the equator, travelled poleward aloft, cooled, grew dense and subsided — which is why the world's great deserts ring this latitude
Cold polar air moving equatorward
Convergence of surface winds
Volcanic activity along the tropics

questions.question: The three semi-permanent anticyclones affecting southern Africa are:
options: Three polar highs
The South Atlantic High, the South Indian High, and the continental or Kalahari High
The ITCZ, the polar front and the doldrums
Three sub-polar lows

questions.question: Cape Town receives its rain in winter because:
options: The ITCZ moves south over the Cape in June
The Kalahari High moves over the Cape
The belts migrate about five degrees north in winter, bringing the westerlies and their cold fronts over the south-western Cape
Cold ocean water evaporates faster in winter

questions.question: The sub-polar low-pressure belt near 60 degrees is significant for South Africa because:
options: It produces the trade winds
It creates the Kalahari Desert
It marks the equatorial rain belt
It is where warm westerlies meet cold polar air along the polar front and rise — the birthplace of the mid-latitude cyclones whose cold fronts cross the Cape

subtopics.title: The Tri-cellular Circulation and the Forces That Bend It

questions.question: The Hadley cell is described as the strongest of the three because:
options: Heat drives it directly — air rises at the equatorial low, moves poleward aloft, subsides at 30 degrees and returns as the trade winds
It is closest to the jet stream
It is turned by its two neighbouring cells
It covers the largest latitude range

questions.question: In the Southern Hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects moving air:
options: To the right, and it is strongest at the equator
To the LEFT; it is zero at the equator, greatest at the poles, and changes direction without changing speed
Downwards toward the surface
Only above 1 000 metres

questions.question: Geostrophic flow occurs when:
options: Wind blows directly across isobars into the low
Friction is at its greatest
Above about a kilometre, friction disappears and the pressure gradient force and Coriolis force balance, so wind blows PARALLEL to straight isobars
The pressure gradient force disappears entirely

questions.question: Buys Ballot's Law applied in the Southern Hemisphere states that:
options: With your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left
Wind always blows from low to high pressure
Lows rotate anticlockwise here
With your back to the wind, low pressure lies on your RIGHT — so lows circulate clockwise and highs anticlockwise

subtopics.title: Air Masses, Berg Winds and Monsoons

questions.question: Air leaving the plateau edge at 1 800 m and 12 degrees Celsius descends to sea level as a berg wind. Its arrival temperature is:
options: 30 degrees Celsius — it warms 1 degree per 100 m, so 1 800 ÷ 100 × 1 = 18 degrees of warming added to 12
12 degrees Celsius, unchanged
21 degrees Celsius
18 degrees Celsius

questions.question: Continental tropical air over the Kalahari is:
options: Cold and moist
Hot and very dry, and it drives South African heatwaves
Cool and humid, bringing east coast rain
Identical to maritime polar air

questions.question: A katabatic (mountain) wind at night explains:
options: Afternoon sea breezes at Durban
The south-east trade winds
Cold dense air draining down-slope and pooling on the valley floor, creating frost hollows and temperature inversions
The formation of the ITCZ

questions.question: The Indian summer monsoon is best explained as:
options: A result of the Coriolis force alone
An ocean current reversal
The migration of the polar front
A sea breeze scaled to a continent — the landmass heats rapidly, a vast thermal low forms, and moist air is drawn in off the ocean as the south-west monsoon

subtopics.title: Hot Air Rises — the Whole Machine in a Kitchen

questions.question: The freezer door spilling cold air at your ankles stands for:
options: A HIGH — cold air is heavy, sinks, and piles up pressing hard on the surface
A LOW
The ITCZ
A cold front

questions.question: The full-taxi and empty-taxi comparison explains:
options: Why air rises
Wind — air flowing from the crowded high to the empty low, and moving faster when the two are close together (packed isobars)
Why deserts form at 30 degrees
The Coriolis force

questions.question: The fogging bathroom mirror and the hair dryer stand for:
options: Land and sea breezes
Trade winds and westerlies
Rising air in a LOW cooling and releasing its moisture as cloud and rain, versus sinking air in a HIGH warming and drying out
Day and night temperature change

questions.question: Why do the world's biggest deserts sit in a ring at about 30 degrees?
options: Air that rose at the equator has cooled and grown heavy by 30 degrees, so it sinks — and sinking air is drying air
There are no oceans at that latitude
The trade winds blow all the moisture away
The jet stream heats the ground there

questions.question: The 'lazy door' in the three-loop picture is:
options: The Hadley cell
The Ferrel cell, between about 30 and 60 degrees — it does not turn itself but is pushed by the cells on either side; its surface wind is the westerlies
The polar cell
The jet stream

questions.question: Jet streams are:
options: Surface winds in the trade wind belt
Ocean currents beneath the polar front
Thin fast rivers of wind high overhead at the joins between the cells, regularly exceeding 200 kilometres per hour
The rising limb of the Hadley cell

questions.question: The sliding of the belts by about five degrees with the overhead sun explains:
options: Why the earth rotates
Why the Coriolis force changes
Why jet streams exist
Why cold fronts reach the Western Cape in winter while wet tropical air pushes into Limpopo and Gauteng in summer — one migration, two rainfall regimes

questions.question: The spinning roundabout comparison shows that the Coriolis force:
options: Is not a push on the air at all — the ground turns underneath the moving air, so its path appears bent
Slows the wind down
Only operates over the ocean
Acts vertically on rising air

questions.question: Standing with your back to the wind in South Africa, low pressure is:
options: Straight ahead
On your RIGHT — from which it follows that lows spin clockwise and highs anticlockwise down here
On your left
Directly behind you

questions.question: A berg wind is scorching and bone-dry because:
options: It picks up heat from the sea
It carries desert sand that heats the air
Falling air is squashed by heavier air below and heats about 1 degree per 100 m — gaining warmth but no water, so relative humidity collapses
It only blows in midsummer

questions.question: In the Simplifier's account, a monsoon is:
options: A type of tropical cyclone
The same thing as a berg wind
A jet stream reaching the surface
An enormous sea breeze that reverses with the SEASON instead of the afternoon — wet air drawn onto the hot summer land, dry air pouring back out over the cold winter land
